title: Oppression, Envy, and the Strength of Two
summary: The Teacher looks at the oppressed, weeping with no one to comfort them, and finds the dead better off than the living. He sees that much labor springs from envy, meets a man who toils alone with no heir and no rest, and praises companionship: two are better than one, and a cord of three strands is not quickly broken. The chapter ends with a story of a poor, wise youth who replaces a foolish old king, only to be forgotten in his turn.
story: Chapter 3 ended with the Teacher seeing injustice and trusting that God will judge. Chapter 4 looks at injustice more closely and more painfully, from the side of its victims. Then it turns to the motives behind human work, the loneliness of the man who works for no one, and the fickleness of political fame. The chapter is a series of observations, each introduced by I saw or again I looked. It adds to the book's portrait of life under the sun, and in the middle of it offers one of the book's clearest goods: the value of companionship.
historical:
The chapter doesn't name a historical setting. Oppression by the powerful was a constant reality in the ancient Near East, whether under Israelite kings, whom the prophets condemned for exploiting the poor, or under the Persian and Greek empires, which many scholars see as the book's setting. The Teacher's observation is not tied to a single regime.

The story of the poor youth and the old king (verses 13 to 16) has prompted many attempts at identification. Interpreters have suggested Joseph, who went from prison to power in Egypt, or David, who replaced Saul, or various later rulers. None of these fits every detail, and the Hebrew of verses 14 to 16 is difficult, leaving unclear exactly who comes from prison and who is the second one. Most interpreters conclude that it is a parable or a general example rather than a reference to a specific historical event.
cultural:
In the ancient world, people without family or patrons had no one to defend them. A comforter was someone who stood beside a person in grief or distress, a role usually filled by family and friends. The oppressed with no comforter (verse 1, stated twice) were truly alone. Verse 8 describes a man with no son or brother, which in that culture meant no heir to carry on his name or receive his property, and no one to care for him in old age.

Verse 11 pictures two people lying together to keep warm, a practical necessity on cold nights for travelers or the poor, who might have only a single cloak. The cord of three strands (verse 12) reflects the rope-making of the day, in which strands were twisted together for strength. Many readers have applied the image to marriage or friendship, though the text itself makes a general point about companionship.
literary: The chapter is a series of observations linked by the Teacher's typical phrases: I saw, again I looked, this too is futile, a pursuit of the wind. It uses several better than sayings (verses 3, 6, 9, 13), a form common in wisdom literature that weighs two things against each other. Verses 5 and 6 set two proverbs side by side: the fool folds his hands and starves, yet one handful with quiet is better than two with toil. Together they chart a middle course between laziness and driven overwork. Verses 9 to 12 build a small argument by examples: falling, keeping warm, and defense against attack, each showing that two are better than one. The number then climbs to three in the closing image.

outline.t: Envy, laziness, and one quiet handful
The lonely man who toils without end
The wise youth and the forgotten king

doctrines.note: The Teacher does not look away from the tears of the oppressed. He names their suffering and their lack of any comforter, and he does not offer a quick answer. Scripture allows the honest recognition of suffering without explaining it away.
Verse 4 traces much human labor and success to envy of one's neighbor. The chapter exposes the hidden motives behind achievement and the damage done by oppression.

The praise of companionship in verses 9 to 12 describes the strength of people bound together. Christians have long applied it to friendship, marriage, and the church, where no one is meant to stand alone.

words.note: Nacham, to comfort or to be sorry. The phrase no comforter appears twice in verse 1. In Isaiah 40 God commands comfort for his people, using the same verb. Here, under the sun, no comforter appears, and the silence is part of the Teacher's lament.

Ashuqim, oppression, from a verb meaning to oppress or extort. The word refers to the abuse of power by the strong against the weak, especially economic exploitation. The Teacher sees it everywhere under the sun.
Echad, one. It appears six times in this chapter. The Teacher contrasts the lonely one who toils without an heir with the strength of two. The repetition emphasizes the vulnerability of being alone.

Hevel, breath, vapor, or futility. It appears four times in this chapter, describing envy-driven labor, the lonely man's toil, and the fickleness of political fame. Each is futile in the sense that it doesn't deliver the lasting gain it seems to promise.

christ: The oppressed of verse 1 have no comforter. Isaiah 40 opens with God's command to comfort his people, and Jesus later promised to send the Holy Spirit, whom John's Gospel calls the Helper or Comforter, so that his followers would not be left as orphans. Jesus also blessed those who mourn, promising that they will be comforted. The chapter's praise of companionship finds a thematic echo in Jesus sending out his disciples two by two and in the New Testament's picture of the church as a body in which no member stands alone. These are connections of theme: Ecclesiastes names the need, and the gospel offers a response.

hard.q: Is it right to say the dead, or those never born, are better off than the living?
hard.a:
Verses 2 and 3 say the Teacher praised the dead above the living, and counted better than both the one who has never existed and so has not seen the evil done under the sun. These are among the darkest words in Scripture. Some readers take them as a considered philosophical position, while others read them as the Teacher's emotional response to seeing overwhelming injustice, the kind of cry also heard in Job 3 and Jeremiah 20, where suffering men curse the day they were born. The Bible includes such cries without endorsing them as final truth; they are honest expressions of anguish, preserved as part of God's word.

The book itself doesn't stay in this place. Later it says that a living dog is better than a dead lion (9:4), and it repeatedly commends life's goods as gifts from God. Readers facing their own despair can find in these verses company rather than a verdict: Scripture knows how dark life can look, and it makes room for that honesty. Anyone for whom such thoughts become a settled wish to die should reach out for help from people who care for them.

questions: The oppressed in verse 1 have no comforter. Who around you is suffering without comfort, and what would it mean to stand beside them?
Verse 4 says much work springs from envy. How much of your own ambition is driven by comparison with others?
Verses 9 to 12 praise companionship. Where in your life do you need to stop working alone?
